title: A Baseball-Sized Robot That Turns Into a Moon Rover
summary:
Space rovers are often big, but a tiny Japanese robot shows small robots may have a big job in space.

The rover is called SORA-Q. Its name comes from the Japanese word sora, meaning "space," the letter Q, for "quest" and "question," and the Japanese word kyu, meaning "sphere." It is about the size and shape of a baseball, and it weighs as much as a cup of water. Once on the moon, it changed into a robot that drove itself around, gathering data.

SORA-Q rode to the moon aboard a probe named SLIM in 2024. SLIM's goal was to test new technology for precise, soft moon landings. SORA-Q's job was to photograph where SLIM landed. After landing, it crawled around for more than 90 minutes, taking pictures.

In ball form, SORA-Q could fit in your palm. It changes shape so each half of the shell becomes a wheel, and a head with cameras pops out. It was inspired by toys, Hirano says.
why_it_matters: Tiny robots like SORA-Q could one day explore caves and craters on the moon that are too tricky for big machines.

background_read: A rover is a robot vehicle that drives around on the moon or a planet, taking pictures where people cannot easily go.
The moon's surface is uneven and covered in dust and craters, which makes driving hard.
Small rovers are cheaper and easier to launch, and they can squeeze into tighter places than big rovers.
Article_Structure: WHO: SORA-Q, a tiny Japanese rover, and engineer Daichi Hirano.
WHAT: SORA-Q changed shape on the moon and took pictures of its lander's touchdown.
WHERE: On the moon, at the SLIM landing site.
WHY: Small rovers can explore tight, risky places more cheaply than big rovers.

perspectives.description: Says small rovers are good for higher-risk and more challenging exploration.
